strengths: Clear and well-motivated gap: existing domain-specific code benchmarks evaluate only what models already know, whereas KoCo-Bench explicitly pairs a knowledge corpus with evaluation tasks, enabling systematic study of how LLMs acquire and apply new domain knowledge. This is a genuine conceptual contribution over EvoCodeBench/DomainEval/MultiCodeBench.

Substantial benchmark construction effort (28.5 person-months, 7 annotators for code tasks, 3 for QA), with a thoughtful pipeline: multi-agent requirement clarification with human-in-the-loop, branch-coverage-driven unit test creation, Docker-verified test suites, and trivial-question filtering using models whose cutoffs predate the dataset.

Comprehensive evaluation: 10 LLMs spanning open/closed-source and cutoff dates, four general specialization methods (SFT, LoRA, RAG, kNN-LM), two code-specific methods (kNM-LM, DSCC), and three coding agents, plus control experiments that address the confound between agent framework and base model (Appendix G).

Careful contamination handling: post-cutoff framework selection, cutoff-labeled models, base models chosen to predate the dataset, and a quantitative contamination index (Table 14), which strengthens the soundness of the low-score findings.

Useful further analyses: continual-learning forgetting across domains (Table 6), corpus-size scaling behavior for SFT/LoRA vs. RAG (Figure 3), error taxonomy with concrete case studies (Figures 4, 6, 7), pass@any upper bounds, seq-length ablation, and performance-cost trade-off analysis. These go beyond typical benchmark papers.

The benchmark targets a realistic and underexplored setting (developing projects on unfamiliar, emerging frameworks such as VeRL, smolagents, Ascend ecosystems) and the error analysis (API hallucination, data constraint violations) is concrete and actionable.
weaknesses: Small evaluation scale limits statistical power: 131 core functions (mean 5.2 per project) and 107 QA items across 6 domains. Domain-level Pass@1 granularity (~18 functions/domain) means individual percentages correspond to 1-2 functions, so claims like 'marginal improvements' or 'inconsistent effectiveness across domains' may partly reflect sampling noise; no statistical significance testing or confidence intervals are reported.

The RAG domain yields 0.0 for all non-agentic baselines; while the authors verify solvability via Claude Code, a domain where every baseline scores zero provides limited signal for differentiating specialization methods and suggests the task-instance selection for that domain may be degenerate for the intended use.

The knowledge corpus is essentially framework documentation + source code + examples - public GitHub material. The framing of 'learning new domain knowledge' is somewhat weakened by the fact that the corpus is not proprietary/unseen in kind, and the contamination analysis (DCI) is only heuristic; the distinction from simply 'a repo-level benchmark with context' could be sharper.

Several important experimental details are thin: RAG uses only BM25 in the main table (dense retrieval relegated to appendix with minimal configuration details), kNN-LM/kNM-LM/DSCC are 'adapted' with few specifics, and Claude Code results depend on a closed-source, black-box agent with terms-of-service restrictions, complicating reproducibility of the headline 34.2% result.

The release link is blank in the submitted PDF; reproducibility cannot be fully verified at review time. Annotation inter-annotator agreement and human-verification criteria for requirements/QA are not reported.

The corpus-size analysis (Figure 3) is correlational over a small number of domain points and conflates corpus size with domain difficulty; the negative correlation for SFT/LoRA ('more data paradoxically hinders learning') is an interesting but under-supported claim.

Novelty is incremental in parts: multi-choice QA for code and test-based code generation evaluation are established; the core novelty rests on the corpus-task pairing, and the paper would benefit from more direct evidence that the benchmark discriminates between (or guides development of) genuinely different specialization approaches rather than uniformly defeating all of them.

strengths: The core idea is well-motivated and genuinely distinguishes KoCo-Bench from prior domain-specific code benchmarks (EvoCodeBench, DomainEval, DomainCodeBench): pairing an explicitly curated knowledge corpus with evaluation tasks enables measuring knowledge *acquisition and application*, not just what models already know. The knowledge-corpus/test-set pairing via software frameworks is a clean, natural design.

Construction is unusually well resourced and documented: 28.5 person-months, 7 annotators, a multi-agent + human-in-the-loop pipeline for requirement clarification, branch-coverage-validated unit tests, Docker-verified execution environments, and a comparison table (Table 2) that transparently situates the benchmark against prior work.

The experimental program is broad and largely well controlled: 10 LLMs with explicit cutoff dates, SFT/LoRA/RAG/kNN-LM plus two code-specific methods, three coding agents, additional dense-RAG and instruction-tuned baselines, a sequence-length ablation, Pass@any upper bounds, contamination detection (CDD), performance-cost analysis, and a control experiment (Appendix G) addressing the base-model confound in agent comparisons.

Honest and informative negative findings: all-zero RAG-domain results manually verified and cross-checked against Claude Code's 62.5%, analysis of why larger LLMs underperform smaller ones, error taxonomy with concrete case studies, and a Limitations section.

Reproducibility is supported in spirit: benchmark, evaluation code, and baselines are stated to be released, and implementation details (hyperparameters, agent tool configurations, decoding settings) are sufficiently specified.
weaknesses: Evaluation granularity is thin. With only 131 core functions (5.2 per project) and 107 QA questions, per-domain Pass@1 cells effectively reflect single-digit task counts (e.g., 5.6% vs 7.6% corresponds to one task difference). No confidence intervals, significance tests, or variance across runs are reported, so many headline comparisons (e.g., specialization methods in Table 4) are statistically fragile.

The knowledge-injection baselines appear under-tuned, weakening the paper's central claims of 'marginal improvements.' SFT/LoRA train on corpus text concatenated and chunked into 2048-token next-token-prediction sequences with no instruction-formatting, curriculum, or retrieval-context variants; RAG uses BM25 with queries built only from function names/signatures. The claims that learning-based methods show *negative* correlation with corpus size and that methods are ineffective may partly reflect weak adaptation rather than fundamental limits; the corpus-size trend in Figure 3 rests on very few points.

Circularity and annotation contamination risks from using Claude Code both as the annotation assistant (test generation, requirement clarification, Q&A generation) and as the top-scoring agent. The authors note human review of all agent-generated content, but no inter-annotator agreement, annotation quality audit, or human-performance ceiling is reported.

A nontrivial portion of headline difficulty may stem from evaluation setup rather than knowledge: all models score 0 on the RAG domain under direct generation, and LLMs (trained cutoffs included) were not given corpus access in the main table, so 'even SOTA LLMs achieve single-digit Pass@1' conflates unfamiliarity with lack of knowledge access; a corpus-in-context prompting baseline for open models is missing from the main comparison.

Positioning and scope: the work is squarely in LLM4SE; relevance to the core ACL/NLP audience is moderate, and the differentiation from closest prior benchmarks is asserted via feature checklists rather than empirically demonstrated (e.g., no experiment showing knowledge-corpus availability changes conclusions on an existing benchmark).

Presentation gaps: the release URL is effectively empty in the manuscript ('at .'), Figure 3 lacks axes/units clarity in the rendered version, and project-level generation—the most realistic task—is relegated to a qualitative appendix study with no quantitative results.

strengths: The paper identifies a genuine and clearly articulated gap: existing domain-specific code benchmarks evaluate what knowledge LLMs already possess, but provide no knowledge corpus to support and evaluate domain specialization (learning/adaptation). The design of pairing a knowledge corpus (framework docs, source code, usage examples) with projects built on those frameworks is a natural and well-motivated construction that directly enables evaluation of SFT/LoRA/RAG/kNN-LM-style methods, which prior benchmarks (EvoCodeBench, DomainEval, etc.) cannot.

The benchmark construction is substantial and rigorously documented (28.5 person-months, 7 annotators, multi-agent requirement clarification with human-in-the-loop, branch-coverage-validated test inputs, Docker-verified test suites). Multi-granularity tasks (function- to project-level generation with unit/integration tests, plus verifiable multiple-choice Q&A) are a sensible design with reliable, non-LLM-judge correctness criteria.

The experimental program is broad and thorough: 10 LLMs with explicit cutoff dates, 4+ domain specialization methods plus adapted code-specific baselines (kNM-LM, DSCC), 3 coding agents, and analyses of continual-learning forgetting, corpus-size scaling, error taxonomy, Pass@any upper bounds, sequence-length ablation, and performance-cost trade-offs. The findings are concrete and actionable.

The paper addresses the obvious confounds proactively: data contamination is handled via cutoff-date design, cutoff-matched base models, and a quantitative contamination index (Appendix H); the agent comparison confound (Claude Code uses Claude Sonnet 4.5) is addressed with control experiments (Appendix G) that preserve the original conclusion; the RAG-domain zero scores are verified manually and confirmed solvable via Claude Code (62.5% Pass@1). This level of self-scrutiny strengthens the validity of the central claims.

Reproducibility support is good: detailed hyperparameters for all specialization methods, agent configurations, evaluation protocol (greedy decoding, Pass@any sampling settings), Docker environments, and a stated release of the benchmark, evaluation code, and baselines.
weaknesses: Scale is modest and per-cell sample sizes are very small: 131 core functions, 25 projects, and only 107 QA questions spread over 6 domains. Many reported Pass@1 values (e.g., 16.7%, 22.2%, 5.6%) imply single-digit function counts per domain, so a single flip changes results by several points. No variance estimates, confidence intervals, or significance tests are reported for any comparison, which weakens claims such as 'marginal improvements' from specialization methods or the cross-domain forgetting effect (Pass@1 7.1% -> 3.6%).

Several conclusions rest on thin evidence: the 'negative correlation between corpus size and SFT/LoRA performance' is drawn from essentially four domain-level points; the continual-learning analysis uses SFT only with no replay/replay-baseline; the error taxonomy is derived from a single base model (Qwen2.5-Coder-7B). These analyses are exploratory but are presented among the paper's headline findings.

The QA construction pipeline filters out questions that three small (7-8B) models answer correctly. This biases the benchmark toward questions that are hard for small models rather than questions that meaningfully probe domain knowledge, and it may inflate the apparent headroom; the effect of this filter on question quality/difficulty distribution is not analyzed.

The agent results (Claude Code 34.2%) depend heavily on a closed, versioned commercial tool whose behavior changes over time, limiting reproducibility of a headline number; also, knowledge-corpus access conditions differ across method families (inference-based methods get project context plus corpus; training-based methods get corpus only), which complicates cross-method comparability.

The resource link in the abstract is empty ('at .'), so the release cannot be verified from the manuscript; anonymity aside, the reviewer cannot confirm the artifact exists, completeness of the released data, or licensing of the third-party framework code included in the knowledge corpus.

Domain coverage is somewhat idiosyncratic (GitHub stars for five Python domains, plus Ascend-hardware frameworks contributed presumably by an industrial sponsor), and Embodied AI / Ascend domains have no code-generation projects at all, so those domains are covered only by QA. The benchmark's generality across domains is therefore uneven.

Related-work comparison (Table 2) is binary checklists that may oversimplify competitors' capabilities (e.g., some existing benchmarks do allow attaching retrieved context), and the claim that existing methods 'provide insufficient gains' is partly asserted from a small set of baselines rather than a systematic study.
